question: Megakernels: fuse the whole forward pass, or delete the idea?

sides.position: Deleted theirs. CUDA Graphs plus PDL recover 98% of the gain, and a megakernel bakes in one model shape and one chip, which breaks as soon as either changes.
Shipping fused decode paths in upstream vLLM, some agent-written and some by hand, for a dozen model and chip pairs. Gains of 1.2 to 2x over the stock engine for one user.

settles_when: Someone runs the same model on the same chip on AgentX with a fused path against a CUDA Graphs plus PDL path, or either camp changes course.
lean: Both, by load. With graph replay on both sides, fused decode won by 1.2 to 2.3x for one user on AMD chips, and the gain shrank as concurrency rose. The price is code: 12 per-model packages and 165k lines. Nobody has yet run fused against graphs plus PDL on one NVIDIA chip.

question: Does accumulated knowledge make the optimising agents better, or worse?

sides.position: Worse. A curated knowledge base cut the final speed-up by about 19%, and expert-written strategies lost to a one-line instruction by about 26%.
Better. A persistent knowledge base is the agent's policy; a skills library raised the ceiling in ablation; search traces train the next model.
Both. Chains that inherit their own reports climb further, and also carry wrong conclusions forward.

settles_when: A second team publishes an ablation of machine-accumulated (not hand-curated) memory on a production-scale task.
lean: The split may be between knowledge people wrote down, which hurts, and knowledge the loop accumulated and can re-test, which helps until it carries an error. That distinction is the whole of the RSI question in miniature.

question: Is this a job for agents, or for plain search?

sides.position: With the same budget, a simple hyperparameter search beat every agent. Agents know the techniques but explore one configuration and stop.
The gains came from new code (kernel fixes, fused paths) that no search over existing knobs could reach.

settles_when: A benchmark separates gains from configuration and gains from new code on the same task, or InferenceBench runs a matched-budget search next to the newest agents.
lean: Both, at different layers. Knobs belong to search; kernels and engine paths belong to agents. The strongest systems already combine them: Together prunes parallelism layouts with a cost model before any agent runs.

question: Is the moat the traffic, or just the harness?

sides.held_by: Inferact, Together, Decagon, an llm-d rollout
sides.position: You need real traffic. Synthetic inputs mislead the agents, nobody can yet simulate traffic they have not seen, and four models sized on public traces reached about 60% of that throughput on their own.
A public set of replayable traces was enough for an academic group with no customers to top the scoreboard.

settles_when: A stack tuned only on the public benchmark is deployed on real traffic and someone reports whether the gains hold.
lean: Toward the traffic, for sizing. Public agent traces overstated four models' capacity by about 1.7x and hid a routing bug. Nobody has yet carried tuning gains, as opposed to capacity, from the public board to real traffic.

question: Does specialisation stop at the workload class, or go down to each customer?

sides.position: Class level is most of it. Tuning a drafter to the coding-agent class was worth about 20%, a general engine came within 6% of a bespoke one, and one hyperscaler rolls each tested fix out to 50 to 100 deployments.
Per deployment, continuously. A bespoke engine now costs a couple of hundred GPU-hours, and one company running the loop on its own traffic reports gains at every layer.

settles_when: A provider publishes per-customer against class-level numbers on the same endpoints.

question: Choose the model once per session, or for every request?

sides.held_by: Databricks, Together, Fireworks, and GitHub until October
sides.position: Once, at the start, or only where no cache is lost: session start, compaction, sub-agent launch. Switching mid-session re-reads the whole context at full price.

sides.held_by: Cursor, OpenRouter, and GitHub since October
sides.position: Every request or turn, with the cost of the cache miss priced into the decision. A session that gets harder should not be stuck on the model it started with.

sides.held_by: Baseten's lab, CacheBridge, Heo and co-authors
sides.position: Make the switch cheap instead. Translate the old model's cache for the new one, 2 to 25x faster than a re-read, for 2 to 8% of accuracy where it works. Research only, open models only.

settles_when: An independent agentic benchmark with caching priced in compares the two on the same tasks. One early result has a trained per-step router halving cost.
lean: Split. A router that prices the cache still kept the same model nine turns in ten, and Fireworks moved from every turn to once per task. GitHub went the other way in October, and Databricks names making the switch cheap as its next step. Translating the cache would loosen this inside a pool of open models; no engine or product does it yet.

question: Is a router worth building, or is a good default model enough?

sides.position: Routing cuts cost by a third to three-quarters at equal quality, by their own measurements, and a perfect choice per task would beat the best single model by 23 points. In November one shipped router was reported ahead of the leading single models on a public agentic board, at lower cost.

sides.held_by: Independent tests, and one vendor's own board
sides.position: No router beat always calling a cheap strong model, several collapsed to one model, and on one vendor's own public board single models from its pool beat its coding router.

settles_when: A vendor publishes its router against the best fixed model in its own pool, on tasks someone else chose.
lean: Still toward a good default model on coding tasks, where single models beat one vendor's router on its own board. But a second vendor now reports its router ahead on a public agentic board, by its own reading and with caching unstated. Live sessions are untested.

question: Tune a model for the job, or wait for the next general one?

sides.position: Tune. On a narrow job it has nearly doubled quality at flat cost, or cut latency by an order of magnitude against a general model.
Wait. A newer general model beat a freshly tuned one on the tuner's own benchmark, a frontier lab is ending self-serve tuning, and a tune dies with its base model.

settles_when: A tuned model is followed against each new general release on the same task for six months.
lean: It depends on how narrow the job is, and it has to be repeated. Harvey's August tune was passed by an untuned general model within three months; tuning four newer bases took the lead back by three points. The wins are on single tasks with their own data and grader; the losses are on general coding, where the next release moves fastest.

question: Does speculation pay less as batches fill, or more?

sides.held_by: Measured tables: Inco AI, UC Berkeley, NVIDIA, Together, Nightjar, Openzeka
sides.position: Less. About 3x for one request falls to 1 to 1.5x at 32 concurrent. On a large mixture-of-experts model the engines' recipe lost from 16 concurrent. A fixed draft length ran up to 30% slower than none at high load.

More, on mixture-of-experts models. A small batch shares few experts, so a guess costs nearly full price; not speculating is close to best at batch 4 and four times worse at 128. Modelled, not measured.

settles_when: Someone measures a mixture-of-experts model in a real engine, with and without speculation, from 1 to 128 concurrent.
lean: Less, on both kinds so far. The first measured mixture-of-experts table, Kimi K3 in two engines, fades like the dense ones: 1.86x for one user, break-even at 16, 0.41x at 64. The modelled rise has not appeared in a real engine; beyond 64 concurrent is still unmeasured.

question: Do looped models save memory, or move it into the cache?

sides.held_by: Ouro's authors, Thinking Machines, No Free Loop
sides.position: Save it. A 1.4B looped model reaches a 4B's reasoning scores with a third of the weights, a looped 26B fits a laptop in about 20 GB, and a loop pays under a fixed parameter budget.
Move it. A cache per pass gives Ouro 1.4B 768 KiB per token, which limits how many sequences a GPU holds. Compressing that cache bought 2.5 to 7.4 times the decoding throughput.

settles_when: A looped and a dense model of equal quality served in the same engine at a provider's batch sizes, with memory and throughput per GPU at several context lengths.
lean: By regime. Saved at batch one on short prompts, the laptop case. Moved on long prompts at serving batch sizes, where agent traffic lives, since Ouro's own tests keep every pass's cache for the prompt. Training-free loops keep the cache size but buy little.
